newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian carmakers face higher taxes in 97/98 budget.
newsitem.headline: Indian carmakers face higher taxes in 97/98 budget.

text.p: Indian carmakers, faced with a slowdown in demand, could be hit by higher taxes on luxury vehicles in the federal budget due this week, analysts said on Monday.
Car sales, hit by slowing industrial growth, grew by a modest 18.5 percent in April-December 1996 over the year-earlier period -- exactly half the pace at which they grew in April-December 1995.
The automobile industry has asked for wide-ranging tax cuts, including a reduction in excise duties on cars, two-wheelers and auto components, but is unlikely to get them, analysts said.

They said excise duties imposed on luxury cars and diesel cars which carry less than six passengers could be raised to 50 percent from the current 40 percent in the 1997/98 (April-March) budget scheduled to be unveiled on February 28.
"We believe such an increase is likely as the revenue implication is significant at three to four billion rupees," ICICI Securities & Finance Company (I-Sec) said in a report.
I-Sec classifies "luxury vehicles" as cars with an engine capacity above 1,200-1,300 cc.
Analysts said a higher tax on diesel cars could be a way to discourage global automobile firms from taking advantage of subsidised, state-controlled product prices.
They said left parties within the coalition United Front government were likely to support the move.

"It was argued that the benefit of subsidy on diesel should not be extended to the wealthy section of society for purchase of luxury vehicle," automobile analyst Jaideep Goswami at UTI Securities said in a report.
Global carmakers, including France's Automobiles Peugeot, Germany's Daimler Benz and Ford Motor Co of the U.S., have already entered the diesel segment.
Goswami said the move to hike taxes on diesel vehicles would be supported by petrol-driven carmakers like Maruti Udyog Ltd.

"This measure would definitely benefit Maruti Udyog as it is handicapped in the absence of suitable deisel versions of its main products," he said. Japan's Suzuki Motor Company and the Indian government each hold 50 percent in the equity of Maruti Udyog, which controls more than 70 percent of the country's car market.
"Increasing taxes on diesel cars would be a disaster," said automobile analyst Rakesh Parekh at Caspian Securities.

"Diesel cars have a higher one-off capital cost and they are more expensive to maintain but consumers are attracted to the segment because of cheaper diesel prices," Parekh said, adding that demand for diesel cars would be hit by such a move.

The industry's wish list includes a cut in excise duties on cars to 30 percent from 40 percent, a reduction in duties on two-wheelers to between 10 and 15 percent from 15 to 25 percent according to engine size and the introduction of a uniform 10 percent duty on auto components.

It has asked the government to spell out a clear policy on the import of completely knocked down (CKD) -- all parts imported for local assembly -- and semi knocked down (SKD) kits. There are no clear guidelines on CKD/SKD packs.

Analysts said the 1996/97 budget -- presented last July -- had been kind to the industry. The government had rationalised excise duties on passenger cars, cut a corporate surcharge to 7.5 percent from 15 percent and extended a subsidy on the purchase of small tractors.
"The industry got a good budget last July, so I'm not expecting much to happen this budget," Caspian's Parekh said.
